newsitem.title: GERMANY: Three Buba council members root for 1999 EMU start.
newsitem.headline: Three Buba council members root for 1999 EMU start.

text.p: Three members of the powerful Bundesbank council stressed on Tuesday that European monetary union would go ahead in 1999, warning however that even Germany could fail to meet every single entry criterion to the letter.

The three senior officials warned of potentially disastrous consequences for the German economy if the planned euro was not created on time, with one even going so far as to admit that loosening the entry criteria could prove to be a lesser evil.
Speaking in Stuttgart, Bundesbank council member Guntram Palm told Reuters in an interview that a postponement of the EMU start would cause more problems than it would solve.
"A postponement is no solution for existing problems," Palm said, adding that a delay could cause the German mark to surge on the currency markets, which would hurt German exports.

Palm also said there was no worry that Germany would miss meeting deficit goals as long as its stuck to its savings course. "A majority of nations are all able to reach the criteria as long as they save assiduously," he said.

His colleague Klaus-Dieter Kuehbacher, speaking at an event in Frankfurt on the Oder, near the Polish border, went one stage further, saying Germany could enter EMU even if it did not strictly meet all the criteria in the Maastricht Treaty.

Countries which want to join EMU in 1999 have to meet targets on interest and exchange rates, inflation, public deficits and debt. Germany, as Europe's largest economy, is seen as an essential founder member of EMU.
Austrian chancellor Viktor Klima told the weekly Die Zeit that EMU without Germany was "not a realistic option". Yet any delay in starting the project could last 10 years, he warned.

For most nations, including Germany, a requirement to cut budget deficits to a reference level of three percent of gross national product is proving the hardest to meet. Economists say Bonn's deficit target of 2.9 percent may be overoptimistic.
Kuehbacher, in his comments, backed this view.

"Germany will not achieve the deficit criterion in 1997," he said. He added: "We don't necessarily have to interpret three percent new borrowing as three-point-zero percent ...Germany should be there from the beginning," he said.
He added that a delay to EMU would be worse than allowing certain convergence criteria in the Maastricht treaty to be interpreted broadly and could undermine the whole project.
In the political arena, European Union leaders meeting in Brussels spoke with one voice in calling for the euro to be launched as planned on January 1, 1999.

Luxembourg's Prime Minister Jean-Claude Juncker said it would not be a good idea to delay the start and both Spanish prime minister Jose Maria Aznar and Ireland's Prime Minister John Bruton said the EMU timetable must be respected.
The third Bundesbank council member, Helmut Hesse, warned in a newspaper interview that a delay in launching the currency would force the whole Maastricht Treaty to be renegotiated.
But he pointed out that this did not mean the Treaty could be ignored completely.
"We must insist the criteria are strictly observed, because the entry of Germany is only allowable under the constitution if the currency union is stable," he told the Nordsee Zeitung.

The strong statements from the central bankers come amid growing market speculation that Europe's monetary union plans are not economically viable -- speculation which governments Europe-wide have done their best to quash.

The comments drive at the very heart of the dilemma Europe's policy-makers face -- the need to keep the momentum going to cut budget deficits as far as possible while at the same time admitting privately that a budget deficit of 3.1 percent might not spell disaster for the entire EMU project.
Under the terms of the Treaty, such a deficit could be allowed if a clause pleading special circumstances were used.
But if financial markets are to be satisified, such clauses must be used sparingly, to avoid the credibility loss which could result from an EMU driven purely by politics.
Yet, as Bank of England governor Eddie George noted on Tuesday, the political commitment to EMU is still paramount, as this provides the adrenalin for unpopular spending cuts.
"The political determination is very strong," George told reporters in Frankfurt after an international meeting.
